newsitem.title: UK: PowerGen outlines overseas project earnings.
newsitem.headline: PowerGen outlines overseas project earnings.

text.p: British electricity generator PowerGen Plc expects to see operating profit of 100 million stg from its existing international projects in five years, group managing director Deryk King said.

King said at a briefing for journalists the operating profits would come from PowerGen's current operations in Germany, Hungary and Australia along with projects under construction in India, Indonesia and Portugal.

PowerGen, which turned in pretax profits of 575 million stg, up from 566 million stg with a dividend of 25.2 pence compared with 21 pence, announced two new projects on Thursday in Indonesia and Thailand.
The new projects would give PowerGen interests in a total 7,700 megawatts of gross generating capacity outside the UK with equity investment by the company of some 700 million stg.

Finance director Peter Hickons said PowerGen, which was frustrated by the British government in its attempt to buy a regional electricity company (Rec) last year, had an efficient balance sheet even though gearing was a "modest" 34 percent.
"I don't think we run an inefficient balance sheet," Hickson said.
"We have a number of projects that we are looking at at any one time. Any one of those projects could substantially increase the gearing," he said.
Hickson added that if the company did not have any further projects, "then we might obviously look at ways in which we could return additional value."
King said PowerGen intended to pursue arrangements with Recs to sell electricity when the domestic market is opened up to competition in 1998.
"Right now, we intend to sell our product to the domestic market through the Recs," he said.
"We believe the Recs will be in a very strong position to defend their electricity business," King said.
But he added that PowerGen was looking at "a multitude of...strategic opportunities," for the future.
Hickson said the company could not comment on the new Labour government's proposed one-off tax on excess profits of privatised utilities.
"Until we see how the legislation is framed, there is very little we can say about it," he said.
PowerGen's colleague National Power said on Wednesday with its annual results that it did not believe it should be covered by any windfall tax and set out arguments to defend its position.
Hickson said he could not comment on National Power's stance.
